title: U.S. House · Virginia's 11th District
area: Most of Fairfax County, Virginia, including the City of Fairfax and the towns of Vienna and Herndon.

context.text: This seat became vacant after Rep. Gerald E. "Gerry" Connolly (D) died on May 21, 2025; James Walkinshaw won the September 9, 2025 special election to fill the remainder of Connolly's term with 75.1% of the vote. Connolly had entered the 2026 Democratic primary before withdrawing (he is listed among the withdrawn candidates); Walkinshaw then advanced unopposed in the 2026 primary after other contenders (Stella Pekarsky, Amy Roma and Bree Fram) also withdrew. Arthur Purves advanced from the Republican primary unopposed after it was canceled. Cook Political Report, Decision Desk, Inside Elections and Sabato's Crystal Ball all rate the race Solid/Safe Democratic as of September 22, 2026.

candidates.name: James Walkinshaw
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the Democratic primary unopposed after other candidates withdrew and the primary was canceled.

summary.text: James Walkinshaw is the Democratic incumbent seeking his first full term representing Virginia's 11th District, having won a 2025 special election after Rep. Gerry Connolly's death. He worked for more than a decade as Connolly's chief of staff and served on the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors from 2020 to 2025. In the House he serves on the Oversight and Government Reform and Homeland Security committees and, according to his official biography, focuses on the federal workforce and government operations.

background.text: Born October 22, 1982, in Arlington, Virginia, and grew up in Prince William County.
Graduated from New York University in 2005 with a B.A. in politics.

Worked in Congress for more than a decade as chief of staff to Rep. Gerry Connolly, advising on federal policy, constituent services and regional priorities such as Metro funding and federal workforce protections; he previously managed Connolly's 2007 and 2008 campaigns.
Served on the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors, representing the Braddock District, from 2020 to September 2025; he chaired the board's Legislative and Environmental committees.

Represented Fairfax County on the Metropolitan Washington Council of Governments, chaired the Regional Transportation Planning Board, and chaired the Virginia Railway Express Operations Board in 2023.

After Rep. Connolly's death in May 2025, won a 10-candidate Democratic primary in June 2025 with about 60% of the vote and then the September 9, 2025 special election over Republican Stewart Whitson; he was sworn in the next day.

In the House, serves on the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (including its Military and Foreign Affairs Subcommittee) and the Committee on Homeland Security. The district includes most of Fairfax County, the City of Fairfax, and the towns of Vienna and Herndon.

Founded and co-chairs the Federal Workforce Caucus with Rep. Steny Hoyer and Sen. Chris Van Hollen; he is also a member of the New Democrat Coalition, the Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition and the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus.
According to his official biography, he lives in Fairfax with his wife, Yvette, and their son, Mateo.

priorities.text: Protecting the nonpartisan civil service and supporting fair pay, benefits and treatment for federal employees.
Strengthening oversight of federal procurement and information technology and holding the administration accountable.

record.text: Serves on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, which oversees the federal workforce, government operations and federal IT management, and on its Military and Foreign Affairs Subcommittee.
Serves on the House Committee on Homeland Security.

candidates.name: Arthur Purves
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the Republican primary unopposed after the primary was canceled.

summary.text: Arthur Purves is the Republican nominee challenging incumbent James Walkinshaw. A retired computer programmer and longtime president of the Fairfax County Taxpayers Alliance, he was the Republican nominee for Virginia State Senate District 32 in 2019. According to his Ballotpedia survey responses, he is running on reducing chronic-disease-driven medical spending, opposing carbon-emissions regulation, and family self-sufficiency.

background.text: According to his Ballotpedia survey response, his family moved to Washington, D.C., in 1953; he graduated from Fairfax County Public Schools and earned a high school diploma from the St. Albans School for Boys.
Received a BA, MBA and MS from the University of Pennsylvania; worked 40 years as a computer programmer.
background.quote: I received a BA, MBA, and MS from the University of Pennsylvania. ... I worked for 40 years as a computer programmer.

background.text: Has served as president of the Fairfax County Taxpayers Alliance for 30 years and treasurer of the Fairfax Committee of 100 for ten years.
Was a member of the 2014 Fairfax County Meals Tax Task Force and has served on the Hunter Mill Citizen Budget Committee.
Ran as the Republican nominee for Virginia State Senate District 32 in 2019, losing to incumbent Janet Howell (73.5% to 26.3%).
Became the Republican nominee for the 11th District after the August 4, 2026 Republican primary was canceled.

Member of the League of Women Voters and the Fairfax branch of the NAACP; has been a Scoutmaster for his church and has taught ESL in Alexandria and at the Tysons-Pimmit Library. According to his survey response, he moved to Vienna 50 years ago and has two children who attended Fairfax County Public Schools.

priorities.text: Reducing federal medical spending by addressing diet-driven chronic disease.
priorities.quote: The federal government spends $2.1 trillion on medical care. Ninety percent is spent on the chronic disease epidemic caused by ultra-processed food and the old high-carb food pyramid.

priorities.text: Opposing state and federal carbon-emissions caps, which he says drive up gas prices.

positions.summary: Opposes carbon caps such as Virginia's participation in the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, saying they raise gas prices, and says the warming trend is not an existential crisis.
Urges a no vote on a proposed Virginia constitutional amendment on abortion, saying it normalizes conception outside of marriage.

summary.text: Dianne Blais is the Green Party candidate on the general-election ballot for Virginia's 11th District. According to Ballotpedia, she has worked as vice-president of a privately held company and holds a B.A. in economics from Mary Washington. Ballotpedia lists no campaign profile, key messages, or campaign finance activity for her.

background.text: Earned a B.A. in economics from Mary Washington.
Professional experience includes working as the vice-president of a privately held company.

researchNotes: Ballotpedia has no staff-curated or survey profile for Walkinshaw beyond his name and party, so his background relies on his official House biography page and Wikipedia; no independent campaign website content was retrieved for him. Blais has no public campaign materials found beyond her ballot listing, so her biography is limited to two facts.
